label: Zeus as sole inherited Olympian
description: Of the Homeric pantheon West credits only Zeus with an Indo-European pedigree; his cognate gods in other branches demonstrate that some theology survived from the common period (developed in Chapter 4).

label: Solar chariot and chariot warfare (post-PIE diffusion)
description: The Sun driving a horse-drawn chariot, and chariot-fighting heroes, appear across many IE traditions, but West argues they spread after the dispersal (spoked chariot c. 2100-2000 BCE), so are not PIE inheritance; cf. Chapter 5.

label: Sacred groves, trees and springs
description: Earliest IE holy places lay in wild nature: groves, sacred trees, springs; Celtic, Germanic, Baltic, Slavonic and Hittite cult sites attest worship of trees and the numinous landscape.

key_terms.term: the Celtic effigy of Zeus is a tall oak

label: Forest deities, singular and plural
description: Woodland divinities fluctuate between one figure and a plurality, often named from words for forest; an Illyrian Vidasus and Norse Víðarr may share a late-IE tree/forest word.

label: Pūṣan and Pan: pastoral god of ways
description: Vedic Pūṣan and Arcadian Pan are equated by name (root 'guard') and function: goat-linked herdsmen's gods, bearded, keen-sighted watchers, protectors of flocks and travellers on roads; a Graeco-Aryan god.

label: Hermes as hypostasis of the way-god
description: Hermes shares Pūṣan's roles: lookout, road god, herd guardian, guide of the dead, leader of the bride, finder of lost or stolen goods, god of gain; 'herma-god' replaced the older name Pan.

label: Nymphs: female spirits of wild places
description: A class of supernatural women haunting waters, trees and mountains is found from India to the Celtic west; despite no shared name, West judges the uniform conception inherited, possibly PIE.

label: Water nymphs and the waters personified
description: Water nymphs embody the waters themselves: Avestan Ahura-wives, Lycian Eliyãna and wedri, Apsarases of the Soma vat paralleled by Greek Nymphs as the water mixed with wine.

key_terms.term: mixed as fourth with three Nymphs

label: Nymphs as daughters of rivers
description: Nymphs are often daughters of rivers or of a water-lord: the Scythian ancestress daughter of the Borysthenes, Ossetic Donbettyr's daughters, Greek daughters of Oceanus, Achelous or Asopus.

label: Nymphs' beauty, song and dance
description: Nymphs are paragons of beauty who sing and dance (and swing in trees); mortals meeting a lovely woman ask if she is a goddess or nymph, and brides are praised as nymph-like.

label: Nymphs cause madness and lead astray
description: Nymphs bewilder minds: Apsarases madden, the nymph-seized are frenzied, Germanic wood-women and Celtic Green Women mislead travellers, Slavonic víly confuse wits and lead men from the path.

label: Unstable unions of nymph and mortal
description: Nymphs take mortal lovers and found lineages, but such marriages never last, often ending when a taboo or condition is broken (Purūravas and Urvaśī, Thetis, Celtic fairy brides, Laumės).

label: Tree nymphs bound to their trees
description: Tree spirits live and die with their trees; Greek hamadryad-type nymphs, Buddhist tree deities, Germanic tree 'mothers' and South Slavonic sprite-trees that may not be cut; nymphs are long-lived but mortal.

label: Child-stealing spirits and changelings
description: Nymphs and elves carry off children or youths and substitute changelings: Greek nymphs, Albanian Jashtēshme, Slavonic víly, Baltic Laumės, Germanic elves, Welsh Fair Folk.

label: Nymph as bride
description: Greek νύμφη means both nymph and bride, and Armenian 'eternal brides' protect brides and young mothers; nymphs are linked with marriage and childbirth.

label: Half-animal beings of the wild
description: Wild beings combine human form with animal parts, especially goat or horse: Indic Kiṃpuruṣas, Greek Satyrs, Sileni, Centaurs and goat-legged Pan, Gallic Dusii, goatish Celtic sprites, Russian lešiy.

label: Captured wild being imparts wisdom
description: A wild creature, often made drunk and bound, reveals useful knowledge: Midas' Silenus, Virgil's Silenus singing a cosmogony, Chiron the educator, the Tirolese Wild Man teaching cheese-making.

label: Dancers and mischief-makers
description: Male sprites of the wild dance and play pranks, stealing and spoiling property: Greek Kouretes, Kerkopes and Kobaloi, Armenian Pay(n), Germanic elves with fairy rings.

key_terms.where: Beings with elements of animal physique

label: Elves
description: Common Germanic elves rank beside gods and men; beautiful, long-lived, musical dancers but tricksters who cause illness ('elf-shot'), tangle hair and steal children.

label: Dwarf smiths and secret craftsmanship
description: Dwarfs live underground and make marvellous things; tales of an unseen smith who works overnight for payment occur in Germany and at Stromboli (Hephaestus); Latvian Rūķis advances men's work.

label: Finger-sized folk
description: Diminutive beings named for fingers or thumbs: Idaean Dactyls as forest finger-people working metal, Pygmaioi, Tom Thumb, Däumling, and Lithuanian Barzdùkai about a finger tall.

label: Elves as artificers; Ṛbhus
description: Elves too can be craftsmen (Volund prince of elves, sun as elf-halo); the Vedic craftsmen Ṛbhus are linked etymologically with 'elf', imperfectly, or alternatively with Orpheus.

label: Giants as a remote race
description: Giants form a class of being dwelling in a distant region, figures of story not cult, strong but dull and aggressive, often extinct and always worsted (Iǫtnar, Gigantes, Nart giants).

label: One-eyed giants
description: Giants are often one-eyed, like the Cyclopes; a Nart story parallels Polyphemus, and one-eyed giants appear in Irish and Lithuanian tales, though West thinks this widespread folk-tale a weak IE candidate.

label: Stone-throwing giants
description: Giants hurl huge rocks: Cyclopes, Laestrygones and Hundred-Handers in Greek, the blind Nart giant, Manx Foawr, Norse sons of Svárang and Hrungnir, German and Lithuanian giants explaining boulders.

label: Many-headed and many-limbed monsters
description: Giants and grotesques have extra heads, arms or bodies: Norse six- and nine-headed giants, Hundred-Handers, Geryoneus, Irish Fomoire, Slavonic Triglav, Saxo's three-bodied giant, six-armed Starkaðr.

label: Giants as builders of ancient works
description: Giants explain huge ruins and landforms: Cyclopean walls of Mycenae and Tiryns, Old English 'work of giants', the giant builder of the Norse gods' wall, Baltic giants' bones and graves, Slavonic osilki.

label: Travellers shelter in a giant's body part
description: Adventurers benighted in Giantland sleep in what seems a cave or hall but is part of a giant (skull, shoulderblade, mitten); dialogue and contests follow; Ossetic and Norse versions suggest a late regional IE tale.

label: Lower mythology: spells, not hymns
description: Spirits of the wild received no regular hymns, being warded off by spells, unlike the way-god honoured with hymns; nymphs fall between, with apotropaic texts but genuine local cults.

label: Heaven and earth as polar pair for the universe
description: Heaven and earth are coupled as a merism for the whole world, often amplified as 'heaven above' and 'earth below'; Germanic alliterating up-heaven with earth.

key_terms.term: nuza sēr nēbis sāit, katanma dēgan sāit

label: Deictic 'this earth, that heaven'
description: Indo-Iranian (and Old English) idiom marking earth and sky with deictic pronouns: this earth, that heaven.

key_terms.term: hya imām būmim adā, hya avam asmānam adā

label: 'All this' as name for the universe
description: The cosmos is called simply 'all this' or 'this whole' in Vedic, Avestan and early Greek philosophical language.

label: Stone sky
description: The word for 'stone' also means 'heaven' in Iranian, suggesting a solid stone firmament in IE belief; Greek Akmon as Ouranos' father; Homeric bronze/iron sky; thunderstones link stone and sky.

label: Cloud word becomes sky word
description: An alternative IE sky-word arose from 'cloud', *nébhes-, which shifted to mean 'sky' in Hittite, Slavonic, Baltic and Celtic.

label: Back of sky, sea, and earth
description: Sky, sea and earth are pictured as having a convex 'back' like an animal, in Vedic, Greek and Old English.

label: Earth's hair = vegetation
description: Vegetation and forests are the earth's or mountains' hair: Vedic, Greek tree-tressed compounds, Norse kennings; a 'hair' word may underlie Norse 'wold'.

label: Earth's bones = stones
description: Stones are the bones of Earth in Norse kennings, an early Greek tragedian, and the Deucalion-Pyrrha myth.

label: Navel of the earth
description: The earth's navel is a sacred site linking to heaven (Vedic fire-pit, Delphi); West doubts inheritance given Hebrew and shamanic parallels.

label: World pillar
description: A prop or pillar holds the sky up: Vedic skambha, Greek pillars beside Atlas, the Saxon Irminsul; possibly IE, possibly borrowed from north-Asian shamanic cosmology.

label: World tree
description: A cosmic tree uniting worlds (Yggdrasil), with Indo-Iranian Soma/Haoma tree and Hesperides' tree as possible analogues; West inclines to Asiatic import.

label: Cosmic serpent of the deep
description: A great serpent dwells in the depths of the waters or encircles the earth: Vedic Serpent of the Deep, Śeṣa, Ophion, Miðgarð Serpent; significance uncertain.

label: Land of the blest at the world's edge
description: Peripheral paradises inhabited by blessed peoples free from sickness and age: Northern Kurus, White Island, Hyperboreans, Isles of the Blest, Irish Land of the Living.

label: Celestial river
description: Rivers flowing in the sky (Sarasvatī, heavenly Ganges, Arədvī), perhaps the Milky Way, may explain the Homeric river-epithet 'flying in the sky'; possibly Graeco-Aryan.

label: Moon as measurer of time
description: The IE moon-word is a masculine 'measurer' also meaning month; feminine 'radiance/light' formations for the moon arose later.

label: Star word
description: The inherited word for star, possibly 'burner', with a collective plural form.

label: The Bear(s) and the Wagon
description: Ursa Major named 'the Bears' goes back to Graeco-Aryan; Latin threshing oxen circling the pole has an Indic parallel; the Wagon name may be Babylonian.

label: Sirius as Triangle Star
description: Avestan Tištrya, Vedic Tiṣíya and possibly Greek Σείριος derive from a 'three-star' formation: a further Graeco-Aryan stellar link.

label: Stars as ornament of the sky
description: The firmament is adorned or embroidered with stars, using the root for adorning/painting in Indo-Iranian, Greek and Latin.

label: Creation as craftsmanship and establishing
description: A divine craftsman fashions the cosmos; the basic IE creation verb means 'set, establish', in Hittite, Iranian, Vedic Dhātṛ and Greek; skilful-artificer epithets in Vedic and Avestan.

label: Creation as birth
description: Alongside making, cosmic origins are told as successive births of world-components, in Hesiod and the Rigveda, compatible with craftsmanship.

label: Negative cosmogony: before heaven and earth
description: Accounts of the beginning list what did not yet exist ('nor heaven above'), in Vedic, Old High German, Norse and Greek, with a primal void/gap.

label: The primal Twin and the dismembered giant
description: A primal 'Twin', apparently self-fertilizing hermaphrodite, is killed by gods and the world made from his body: Ymir, Tuisto, Yama/Yima, Purusha, possibly Remus.

label: Primal cow/ox in cosmogony
description: A primal bovine accompanies the first being (Norse Auðhumla, Iranian primal ox); cosmogonic cow-sacrifice is securely attested only in Iranian.

label: Numbered canons
description: Precepts and lore codified as 'there are three (or n) things', then enumerated: Indic, Avestan, Greek, Irish, Welsh triads.

label: Catechism by question and answer
description: Wisdom delivered by sage or god in answer to formulaic questions ('I ask thee, tell me'), in Avestan, Vedic and Eddic poetry.

key_terms.term: tat͂θβā pərəsā, ərəš mōi vaocā, Ahurā

label: Superlative questions: what is best?
description: Questions and gnomic answers about the best, greatest or most of things, in Avestan, Homeric, Pythagorean, Hesiodic, Indic, Norse and Old English material.

label: Proverbs
description: Cross-branch proverb matches exist, but borrowing and independent invention make reconstruction of IE proverbs doubtful.

label: Riddle contests and life-and-death riddles
description: Riddles as serious tests posed by monsters, suitors or rival seers; contests of riddling and mythological knowledge (Mopsus and Calchas, Heidrek, Vafthrudnir).

label: Riddling poetic code
description: Poetic metaphor is a systematic code (sets as brothers/sisters, flyers as birds, nourishers as cows) shared by riddle and hymn.

label: Fire devours its parents
description: Riddle of the child that devours its mother(s): fire consuming the kindling wood, Vedic and Hesiodic; at least Graeco-Aryan.

label: 'I saw' riddle opening
description: Riddles introduced as something the propounder saw, common to Vedic, Greek, Persian, Germanic and Slavonic.

label: Self-describing and dead-voice riddles
description: Riddles where the dead creature speaks through an instrument (horn, conch), and first-person self-descriptions; antiquity uncertain.

key_terms.term: κνήμηι νεκρὸς ὄνος με κερασφόρωι οὖας ἔκρουσεν

label: Two-, three-, four-footed: the man with a stick
description: The Sphinx riddle draws on the IE two-footed/four-footed antithesis; 'three-footed' for an old man with a stick is an inherited locution.

key_terms.term: trydyd troet y hen y ffon

label: X and not-X riddles; neither-nor conditions
description: Riddles of things that are and are not X, 'without' series, and tales of impossible polar conditions fulfilled by intermediates.

key_terms.term: αἶνός τίς ἐστιν ὡς ἀνήρ τε κοὐκ ἀνήρ

label: Year as wheel
description: The year is a revolving wheel or wheeled vehicle with numbered spokes for its subdivisions; Greek 'as the years revolved' presupposes it.

label: Year as father; Day and Night as sisters
description: Genealogical year-riddles: a father with twelve sons and 720 children; Day and Night as sisters or mother-daughter.

key_terms.term: Two sisters who are at odds

label: Days as cattle
description: Days or dawns pictured as cows; the Sun's herds in the Odyssey (350 cows, 350 sheep) were originally a riddle for days and nights of the year.

key_terms.term: three hundred and sixty milking cows

label: Cosmic weaving by Day and Night
description: Day and Night (or Sun and Moon) weave the sky's fabric on a loom, alternating black and white threads; echoes in Vedic, Greek, Latvian.

label: King distinct from war-leader/hero
description: Early IE societies separate the king (remembered for justice, prosperity, generosity) from the outstanding hero or elected war-leader who fights on his behalf.

key_terms.term: Reges ex nobilitate, duces ex uirtute sumunt

label: King and queen titles from *(H)regˆ
description: Indo-Iranian and Celtic preserve the old words for king and queen, derived from a root meaning to make straight, direct, rule; survivals at the periphery of the IE world.

label: King as straightener; straight justice
description: The king is conceived as one who makes things run straight; the straight vs. crooked opposition underlies terms and images for justice and governing.

label: Elective kingship; heir as second after the king
description: Kingship seems originally elective within limited families, depending on armed men's support; Iranian and Irish heirs presumptive bore a title meaning second after the king.

label: Kingdom comes with a woman; marriage to Sovereignty
description: A man becomes king by marrying a queen or royal widow/daughter; in Irish legend the king weds a goddess embodying Sovereignty or the land itself.

label: Mead-queen and the drink of sovereignty
description: Medb and Mādhavī, both named from mead, pass through successive royal husbands; a ritual drink confers sovereignty on the new king.

label: Queen's ritual mating for the community
description: In royal ritual the queen undergoes a sacred coupling with a god or sacrificial animal: Athenian queen and Dionysus, Indian queen with the Aśvamedha stallion.

label: Royal horse sacrifice and king's union with the mare
description: Kingship rituals involve horse sacrifice: the Indian Aśvamedha, an Irish inauguration with a mare, the Roman October Horse, and the Swedish king's horse feast.

label: The one-shoe man as claimant to rule
description: Irish custom of the inaugurated claimant receiving back a deposited shoe may explain Jason the single-sandalled rightful claimant in Greek myth.

label: King paired with high priest; priestly titles
description: Beside the king stands a high-status priest with possibly cognate titles in India and Rome, and other priestly titles match across Indo-Iranian and Europe; priests wore white.

label: King as charioteer or helmsman
description: The ruler guides the community as a driver steers a chariot or a helmsman a ship, in Vedic, Irish, Greek, and Indian epic sources.

label: King as father to his people
description: The good king protects his subjects as a gentle father, under whom they live like sons in their father's house (Greek and Indian epic).

label: King as herdsman of the people
description: The ruler is styled the herdsman or shepherd of his people in Vedic, Homeric, Old English and Old Saxon poetry.

label: Ideal king: eloquent, handsome, wise judge
description: The ideal ruler is eloquent, of fine appearance and the source of justice, rendering right judgments; Greek, Avestan and Irish evidence.

label: Corrupt king 'eats' gifts or people
description: A bribe-taking or exploitative ruler is said to eat gifts or devour his people: Hittite parable, Greek epithets, a Rigvedic simile.

label: King's justice ensures the land's fertility
description: A just ruler brings timely rain, crops, milk, fish and offspring; an unjust one blights nature and may be deposed or sacrificed (Indian, Iranian, Greek, Norse, Celtic).

label: King as giver of rings and treasure
description: The king accumulates and redistributes wealth (horses, cattle, gold rings) to heroes and poets; Germanic kennings call him ring-giver or treasure-breaker.

label: King gives away his eye
description: Indic and Irish myths show supreme royal generosity: a king surrenders his eye(s) to a petitioner and is divinely restored.

label: Hero's colossal size and strength
description: Old heroes were giants of prodigious strength, lifting stones beyond present-day men or working doors several men need; Homer suppresses but retains traces.

label: Hero breaks weapons, chariots, horses until one holds
description: The young hero tests and breaks equipment until only a chief's own arms or a single horse withstand his strength (Irish, Iranian, Armenian).

label: Band of helpers with single marvellous faculties
description: Adventurers with individual wondrous talents (swift runner, far-seer) aid a quest, the Helfermärchen type; ancient but not claimed IE by West.

label: Hero's fair hair and flashing eyes
description: The heroic infant is marked by blond/golden hair and piercing bright eyes, a stock feature in Greek, Germanic, Irish and Welsh tradition.

label: Hero grows at a multiple of normal rate
description: The child hero grows miraculously fast, typically said to grow in a day or month what others grow in a year (Irish, Welsh, Persian, Armenian, Ossetic, Serbo-Croat).

label: Boyhood feats against animals; outrunning deer
description: Before war, the boy hero proves himself against animals: strangling snakes, killing lions and boars, outrunning and catching deer barehanded (Greek, Indian, Irish, Welsh, Caucasian, Norse).

label: Precocious first kills at seven or twelve
description: Heroes begin killing men very young, at seven in Norse and Irish sources or at twelve in Norse and Serbo-Croat tradition.

label: Adult hero against a unique beast (great boar hunt)
description: The grown hero must overcome an exceptional animal of a familiar kind; the great boar hunt is prominent in Greek, Welsh and Irish saga.

label: Heroic dragon-slaying derived from the cosmic myth
description: Heroes kill dragons or monsters, sometimes to save a princess or win treasure; West suggests the heroic feat derives from the thunder-god's serpent-slaying.

label: Asking a stranger's identity and lineage
description: On meeting an unknown person, especially a battle opponent, the hero asks who he is and of whom/whence; a typical double question in many traditions.

label: 'Are you a goddess?' to a beautiful woman
description: A man meeting a lovely woman in Greek or Indian epic wonders aloud whether she is a goddess or other supernatural being.

label: 'Fool or from far away' retort to a newcomer
description: A stranger's naive question draws the reply that he is either a simpleton or from far away (Odyssey and Mabinogion); West deems it a coincidence, not proof.

key_terms.term: νήπιός εἰς, ὦ ξεῖν̓, ἢ τηλόθεν εἰλήλουθας
ae tydi yn wr o bell, ae titheu yn ynuyt

label: Hero aloof from women and sex
description: The IE warrior hero is mostly unmarried and uninvolved with women; women matter functionally only as a bride to be won or a wife to be regained.

label: Bride contest with death for failed suitors
description: A desirable woman is won only through a contest in which unsuccessful suitors forfeit their lives (Greek, Danish, Nart).

label: Self-choice: bride chooses by garland
description: In a svayaṃvara the bride picks among assembled suitors, signifying choice with a garland or flowers (India, Helen in Greece, Iran, Latvia, Germany); West sees an IE tradition, perhaps seasonal.

label: Bride chooses by giving a cup
description: A variant of self-choice in which the bride hands a cup of wine to her chosen suitor (Scythian and Celtic accounts), recalling Celtic marriage and sovereignty drinks.

label: Bow-stringing contest for a bride
description: Suitors must string a mighty bow (Indian epics, Penelope's contest); West hesitates to call it IE, linking it to the steppe composite bow.

label: Suitors race for the bride
description: Suitors compete in races for brides (Danaids, Antaios, Ikarios), which West relates to seasonal ritual sports like racing to the Maypole.

label: Sword (barrier) in the bed
description: A couple sleeps with a sword or other object between them to guarantee chastity; the sword postdates PIE, but a bed barrier existed in Gaelic and Indian custom.

label: Abducted wife recovered by force; legitimate abduction
description: A wife's abduction requires her husband's armed recovery; Jamison's Indo-Greek pattern of legal versus illegal capture, which West would call Graeco-Aryan.

label: Husband's Return (not IE)
description: The long-absent hero returns in disguise as his wife is to remarry and wins her back; West treats it as a wandering folk-tale from the steppes (Alpamysh), not IE.

label: Hero's son as substitute or avenger
description: A hero's son rarely fights beside him; he defends, replaces or avenges his father (Telemachus, Neoptolemus, Orestes).

label: Father-son combat (Sohrab and Rustum)
description: Father and son, raised apart, meet unrecognized and fight, one killing the other; attested across Iran, Greece, India, Germany, Ireland, Russia, Armenia, Ossetia, though perhaps diffused.

label: Thyestes motif: children served as food
description: An enemy kills a man's children and serves them to him to eat (Greek, Norse, Ossetic); the Caucasian case argues against Classical borrowing.
sections: The hero’s child as object of pathos

key_terms.where: The hero’s child as object of pathos

The hero’s child as object of pathos

label: Archery feat endangering the hero's child
description: A father must shoot at a target on his child without harming him (Lycian Sarpedon story, William Tell, Norse sagas).
sections: The hero’s child as object of pathos

key_terms.where: The hero’s child as object of pathos
The hero’s child as object of pathos

label: Hero slain in his bath
description: The formidable hero is killed when defenceless in the bath (Agamemnon, Irish Con Roí, Saxo's Olo).

label: Hero kills monster but dies of its venom
description: The hero's honourable death comes from dispatching a monster and dying of its poison or wounds (Beowulf, Thor at Ragnarøk, Fergus, Heracles' Hydra venom).

label: Invulnerable hero buried under earth or stones
description: Heroes impervious to weapons are overcome by strangling or by being buried under earth or stoned (Kaineus, Ajax, Sorli and Hamdir, Sosruquo).

label: Invulnerable hero's single weak spot
description: An otherwise invulnerable hero has one vulnerable spot, usually ankle, heel, foot or leg (Achilles, Talos, Krishna, Soslan, Siegfried, Conganchnes, Diarmaid).

label: Inherited word for 'sun' and its gender
description: The MIE sun-word is an l/n heteroclite neuter, later personalized as masculine or feminine; West suggests it originally meant 'lamp', perhaps 'the lamp of Dyeus', and may be a loan.

label: The Sun as a god
description: Across most branches the Sun is recognized as a deity with names, cult, genealogy and personified roles, male in the south, often female in the north.

label: Great and swift Sun
description: The Sun bears the epithets 'great' and 'swift' with cognate adjectives in Vedic and Greek, and rises to give light to all beings, gods and men.

label: The all-seeing Sun, watcher of gods and men
description: The Sun surveys the whole world and sees all deeds, right and wrong; he is the spy or watcher of all, expressed with the cognate root of spáś-/σκοπός.

label: Sun as eye of god; eye as sun
description: The Sun is called the eye of the gods or of a god (Varuna, Mitra-Varuna, Ahura Mazda, Jupiter, God); conversely human eyes are likened to suns, and Irish súil 'eye' may be the sun-word.

label: Sun as keeper of cosmic order and witness of oaths
description: The Sun obeys fixed cosmic law and, because he sees all, serves as justice's eye and is invoked as witness to oaths and treaties in Hittite, Greek, Iranian, Armenian, Germanic and Irish tradition.

label: The solar wheel
description: The sun is conceived as a wheel rolled or driven across the sky, with the inherited phrase 'wheel of the sun' expressed through two old wheel-words; spoked wheels and swastikas are widespread solar symbols.

label: Sun's horse(s) and chariot
description: The solar wheel is drawn by a horse, then becomes a one-wheeled or ordinary chariot with a team of horses; attested in Vedic, Avestan, Greek, Norse, Irish, Baltic and Slavic tradition and Bronze Age art (Trundholm).

label: The solar boat and night ferry
description: A boat, ship or bowl carries the Sun, often by night over the ocean, combined with the daytime horse-drawn vehicle; Vedic, Bronze Age Scandinavian, Greek and Latvian evidence.

label: The dark side of the sun
description: Vedic doctrine that the sun has a bright and a dark face, returning unseen eastward at night; West suggests the gilded and dull faces of the Trundholm disc reflect the same idea.

The dark side of the sun

label: Dating the solar chariot myth
description: The sun-boat may be ancient, but the horse-drawn chariot myth cannot be PIE since the spoked wheel is late; it spread with chariot warfare across already diverging IE peoples, and was borrowed by Egypt and China.

label: The Sun's tireless round, rest and bath
description: The Sun never tires or rests in his daily journey, yet sleeps or rests at night; he bathes in Ocean or the sea to emerge clean at dawn (Greek, Baltic, Slavonic, Celtic).

label: Solar festivals imitating the sun
description: Calendrical solar festivals imitate the sun: discs carried or drawn in procession, fire wheels rolled downhill, bonfires, and sun-shaped cakes (Vājapeya, Solmonath, hot cross buns).

label: Ritual swinging and solar dancing
description: Swinging at spring and midsummer festivals symbolizes the sun's changing declination; the Sun is believed to dance at Easter or midsummer, and ring-dances mirror its circling.

label: Salutation of the rising and setting sun
description: Daily greeting of the sun at rising and setting is attested over most of the IE area: Gāyatrī prayer, Greek hand-kissing, Persian prayers, Nordic, Baltic, Bavarian and Scots Gaelic customs.

label: Taboo on urinating towards the sun
description: Hesiod, Pythagoreans, the Magi and Indian law-books forbid urinating facing the sun, and some also standing upright; West regards the verbal match as too natural to be a formula.

label: Dawn goddess and her name
description: Dawn's name continues an IE root for red glow, and she is a goddess in Vedic, Avestan, Greek, Germanic and Baltic tradition; West detects her also behind Brigantia and St Brigit.

label: Dawn born daily, daughter of Heaven
description: Dawn's appearance is a birth repeated daily; she is the daughter of Dyaus/Zeus, a title shared with the Lithuanian Sun-goddess and reflected in Eos' epithets δῖα and ἠριγένεια and Brigit's birth.

label: Dawn immortal, shining and wide-shining
description: Dawn is unageing and immortal and above all shines, with the cognate root bhā/φα- in Vedic, Avestan and Greek; 'shines widely' and 'much-seeing' Dawn are also matched.

label: Dawn's fingers, arms, golden hue and garments
description: Dawn's rays are pictured as fingers or arms, rosy or golden; she is gold-coloured, robed in light or saffron, and gold-sandalled, with parallels in Vedic Savitṛ and Latvian Saule.

label: Dawn's seductive display, smile and dancing
description: Uṣas bares her breasts like a courtesan and smiles enticingly, perhaps once true of Eos too (Aphrodite's 'laughter-loving' epithet); Dawn dances and has dancing-places in the east.

label: Dawn's house and the doors of Heaven
description: Dawn has a house in the east and opens the doors of Heaven with her light; Avestan 'Dawn-house' mountain and the Latvian 'doors of the house of God' are comparable.

label: Dawn and Night as alternating sisters
description: Dawn and Night are sisters who alternate on one road, never meeting; Hesiod's house of Night with its threshold, Parmenides' gates of Night and Day, and a Latvian riddle closely parallel the Vedic picture.

label: Dawn's horses and chariot
description: The Sun's horses and chariot are transferred to Dawn, often white-horsed, while Night has dark horses; Vedic, Avestan, Greek and Norse evidence.

label: Dawn rouses people to their work
description: Dawn wakes all living things and sets people on the road and oxen to the yoke, in Vedic, Gathic and Hesiodic passages.

key_terms.term: Dawn forwards the journey, forwards the task

label: Dawns and days as cows; milking imagery
description: Dawn's rays are red cows, dawns are cows, Day and Night are white and black cows or bulls; the Sun's cattle in the Odyssey represent days and nights, and νυκτὸς ἀμολγῶι preserves the image.

label: Dawn's lovers
description: Eos carries off handsome mortal youths such as Tithonos; Uṣas is erotically alluring, the Sun is her lover, and the contrast between ageless Dawn and ageing men is noted in Vedic texts.

label: Dawn goddess and the spring festival
description: Though daily, the Dawn goddess became attached to spring festivals in some branches: Eostre/Ôstara and Easter, the Spartan Aotis, Erigone of the Aiorai, and Mater Matuta's Matralia.

label: Daughter of the Sun and the Divine Twins
description: The Sun's daughter is wooed by or rides with the twin horsemen: Sūryā with the Aśvins, the Baltic Saules meita with the Sons of God; she is the model bride in wedding songs.

label: Rival suitors of the Sun-maiden; astronomical readings
description: Rivalry for the Sun's daughter involves Moon, Morning Star, thunder-god; promises broken and feasts disrupted; West reads these as romantic interpretations of celestial movements but without exact astronomical meaning.

label: Helen as Greek Daughter of the Sun
description: Helen, sister of the Dioskouroi, daughter of Zeus, worshipped as goddess, with a name *Swelénā linked to sun-words, egg-birth and corposants, continues the Sun-maiden; the Leukippides are another version.

label: Abduction of the Sun-maiden
description: Repeated abduction and recovery of the Sun-maiden: Helen by Theseus and by Paris with the Atreidai as paired brothers; the Ossetic Aziruxs; Guinevere abducted on May morning.
sections: Daughters of the Sun in other traditions

key_terms.where: Daughters of the Sun in other traditions

label: Sun-maiden's wedding mirrored in May customs
description: Myth of the Sun's daughter's wedding reflects spring/summer rites: decorated May-trees, eggs, ring-dances, swinging songs, May Queen and bride auctions, races to the Maypole, Helen's Spartan wedding festival and tree cult.

label: Sky-god *Dyeus
description: The deified bright sky, reconstructed with an archaic declension shared by Vedic and Greek and reflected across Italic, Illyrian, Thracian, Anatolian; a sky/day entity and father of gods, not originally a ruler or storm-god.

label: Great Heaven
description: The sky's vastness expressed by 'great' epithets of Heaven and the sky-god in Vedic and Greek.

label: Rain of the sky-god
description: Rain conceived as coming from the sky-god, expressed in parallel genitive collocations in Greek and Vedic; rain also as Dyaus' seed.

label: House and door of the sky-god
description: Heaven pictured as the god's dwelling with a house and doors, where gods gather or the dead go; Greek, Vedic and Latvian parallels.

label: Father Sky
description: The sky-god's most constant title is 'father', in fixed vocative and nominative combinations in Vedic, Greek, Italic, Illyrian, Baltic and hypocoristic Anatolian forms; the combination is traced back to PIE.

label: All-seeing, all-knowing sky god
description: Omniscience and wide vision belong to sky and celestial gods who survey the world; in Indo-Iranian this passes to Varuna, Mitra, Ahura Mazdā, Mithra, with watchers or spies supervising justice.

label: Divine watchers and spies
description: The justice-supervising celestial god has myriad watchers, spies or eyes roaming the earth (Zeus' watchers, Varuna's thousand-eyed spies, Mithra's ten thousand spies).

label: Sky-god as witness to oaths
description: The deified sky naturally witnesses oaths: Dius Fidius taking oaths under open sky, Greek asseveration 'let Zeus know it', a possible Germanic parallel, and a Luwian oath deity.

label: Father of gods and men / All-father
description: The sky-father as universal father of gods and men; Odin inherits the title (All-father) and the high-seat survey of all worlds, though classical influence may be suspected.
sections: Sky and Earth as a pair

label: Eyes of the sky
description: Sun and moon as the eyes of Dyaus, with an etymological match in the Homeric 'eyes of Zeus' and the Latvian 'eye of God'.

label: Divine Earth *dʰég̯ ʰom-
description: The PIE earth noun with holodynamic inflection survives widely and was originally animate, personified as a goddess under direct reflexes, suffixed forms or other names (Hittite, Greek, Thracian, Lithuanian, Roman).

label: Earth as 'the Broad One'
description: A kenning for Earth meaning 'the Broad One' yields goddess names and earth words in Vedic, Greek, Germanic and perhaps Gaulish.

label: Mother Earth
description: Earth widely titled 'mother': Hittite, Vedic, Greek (all-mother, mother of gods), Demeter, Germanic Nerthus and Anglo-Saxon charms, Slavonic, Latvian 'Mother of Earth', Celtic Ana.

label: Mother Moist Earth
description: Slavonic formulaic title of Earth as moist mother; Earth invoked in oaths and land disputes, perhaps paralleled by Solon.

label: Humans as children of Earth
description: Mankind as earth-born children of one mother Earth: Armenian earth-born men, Cædmon's children of Earth, Latvian and Pindaric 'one mother', lineages traced to Earth.

label: Earth fertile and pregnant
description: Earth as a living, pregnant mother who gives birth to plants and feeds all; digging forbidden while she is pregnant; fertility of fields.

label: Broad earth
description: 'Broad' is the commonest Indo-European epithet of earth, with Greek-Vedic etymological matches and an Indo-Iranian formula, plus Germanic analogues in other vocabulary.

label: Earth as broad seat
description: Heaven and earth as the 'seats' of gods and mortals; broad-seated earth in Vedic and Greek.

label: All-bearing, all-nourishing earth
description: Earth bears and nourishes all creatures, expressed with 'all'-compounds (Vedic viśva-, Greek παν-) and the verb 'bear' in Indo-Iranian and Greek.

label: Dark/black earth
description: Earth as dark or black, a frequent Hittite formula and current in Greek, Irish, Slavonic and Lithuanian, often tied to death and the underworld.

label: Earth receives the dead
description: With inhumation the dead return to Mother Earth, who enfolds them in her lap or garment-folds; Earth goddesses preside over the dead (Vedic, Greek, Roman, Baltic).

label: Heaven and Earth as divine pair and parents
description: Sky-father and Earth-mother paired as primeval, universal parents of gods and all life; clearest in Vedic, broken up in Greek (Ouranos/Gaia), with Hittite, Roman, Norse traces.

description: At the first furrow the farmer prays that Mother Earth with Father Sky's aid will bear a heavy crop: Anglo-Saxon field charm and Hesiod's prayer to Zeus Chthonios and Demeter.

label: Sky as bull, Earth as cow
description: Heaven and Earth represented as bull and cow; Dyaus the bellowing bull whose seed is rain, Zeus as bull with cow-partners (Europa, Io), Latvian God's bulls, Russian riddle.

label: Cattle as reference point
description: Cattle as wealth on a par with wives, metaphors for kin, rulers as cowherds, value units, and times of day named after cattle activities.

label: Dawn as daughter of the sky-god
description: The dawn goddess is pre-eminently the Sky's daughter in Vedic, with traces in Greek Eos' epithet and Baltic; assigned to Graeco-Aryan and probably MIE.

label: Celestial gods as children of Dyaus
description: Sky-related gods (Agni, Sūrya, Indra, Parjanya, Maruts) loosely called Dyaus' offspring.

label: Divine Twins, Sons of *Dyeus
description: Vedic Aśvins, Greek Dioskouroi and Baltic Sons of God continue an MIE pair of divine twins, youthful sons of the sky-god.

label: Twins as horsemen
description: The twins are associated with horses (often white), golden chariots and riding; good-horsed epithets matched; horse-named twin pairs elsewhere.

label: Twins as rescuers at sea and in battle
description: The twins are bright, winged saviours who bring light and rescue men from drowning and battle; Baltic Sons of God urged to save the Sun's daughter.

label: Twins and dawn/Sun's daughter
description: Twins tied to morning and the Dawn or Sun's daughter, their sister or companion (Uṣas, Helen, Baltic Daughter of the Sun).

label: Other twin reflexes
description: Further possible divine-twin pairs: Theban and other Greek twins, Celtic Dioskouroi from the Ocean, Germanic Alcis and migration-leader brothers, artistic twin figures, the Spartan dokana.

label: Sky-father's motherless children
description: Dawn and the Twins have no link with Earth; their affinity is with the sky alone, and no mother need be posited, as with mythical parthenogenesis.

label: Consort *Diwōnā
description: Dunkel's hypothesized sky-god's spouse named by suffixation from his name, seen in Dione, Mycenaean di-u-ja and Dia; transfer to Hera/Indrāṇī.

label: Horse-metamorphosis birth myth
description: Greek Dia/Ixion story and Indian Saraṇyū myth share immortal bride and mortal groom, a substitute wife, horse transformation and equine offspring.

label: Earth as consort of *Dyeus (χθὼν δῖα)
description: The epithet 'belonging to Zeus' on earth may reflect an older pairing of Earth with *Dyeus, later extended to sea, air and goddesses.

label: Primal 'Man' ancestor of mankind
description: Germanic Mannus and Indic Manu, both from the word for 'man', reflect a shared prototype: a first Man from whom all humans descend; possible traces in Iran and Anatolia.

label: Humans born from Earth or trees
description: Mankind, children of Mother Earth, is imagined as growing from the soil or from trees, especially the ash: Hesiod's Bronze Race, Pelasgus, Tuisto, Norse Askr and Embla, Iranian rhubarb-born first couple.

label: Twin figure and the first mortal / king of the dead
description: The cosmogonic Twin (Ymir, Tuisto, Yama/Yima) survives in Indo-Iranian chiefly as the first to choose death, founder of the path of the dead, or paradisal world-ruler; Gauls descended from Dis pater.

label: Divine descent of noble lineages
description: Separation of gods and men is incomplete: Rishis, Greek heroes, Scythian, Roman and Germanic royal houses claim descent from gods, a practice West thinks may go back to Indo-European times.

label: Ideal lifespan of a hundred years
description: The ideal human life is a hundred years ('a hundred autumns'), seen in Vedic prayers, Latin saeculum and Welsh hoedl 'lifetime', an Irish hymn, and Lithuanian christening toasts.

label: Quest through ever-older animals
description: A seeker consults a chain of progressively older creatures (owl, crane, tortoise; ouzel, stag, owl, eagle, salmon) to recover lost knowledge; Mahābhārata and Culhwch and Olwen share the distinctive pattern, implying common inheritance.

label: Birth-attending Fate goddesses who spin
description: Female figures, often a trio, attend each birth and fix the child's life-span and fortune, typically by spinning its thread; found across Europe and Bronze Age Anatolia, likely deep Indo-European.

label: Life as a thread or warp
description: Even without spinster goddesses, Vedic texts picture lineage and life as an extended thread or warp on a loom; Irish sea-daughters 'fashion the threads'; Baltic and Slavic threads snap at death.

label: Fate as turning / becoming (Wyrd, Urð)
description: Germanic fate words (Urð, wurth, Wyrd) derive from the root 'turn/become', linking eventuating with the turning spindle; spindle-whorl words share the root across languages.

label: Past, present and future as totality
description: The Norns Urð, Verðandi, Skuld and Plato's Moirai cover past, present and future, applying an inherited (at least Graeco-Aryan) totality expression to the Fates' sway.

label: Fate woven as a web
description: Spun life-threads are woven into a larger fabric: Norns fasten Helgi's threads across the world, Valkyries weave battle, Old English 'webs of war-success'; Norse fate words from a root 'weave'.

label: Destiny fixed by utterance (and writing)
description: Fate is fixed by pronouncement, like a king's word (fatum, θέσφατον, Morta profata, Lithuanian Laima lėmė); the writing image is a later independent development, not Indo-European.

label: Dying by one's own death
description: A widespread idiom distinguishes a natural death 'by one's own death' from a violent, alien one, attested from Greek and Latin to Old Persian, Pali, Ossetic, Baltic and Slavic.

label: Death as sleep
description: Death is euphemised as sleep (Vedic 'put to sleep' for killing, Homer's bronze sleep, Lucretius, Norse sofa, Old English swefan); West notes the image is not distinctively Indo-European.

label: The road of no return
description: The journey of the dead is the way of no return, in Indian epic, Greek and Latin poetry, Ossetic and Hittite texts, though Near Eastern parallels make it not distinctively Indo-European.
sections: Death as sleep; death as a journey

label: Crossing the water to the dead
description: A river, lake or sea separates the living from the dead, crossed by ford, ferry or ship: Vaitaranī, Acheron and Charon, Latin tarentum 'crossing-place', Slavic and Baltic fare-coins, ship burial.

label: Bridge of the dead
description: Some traditions place a bridge on the way to the otherworld: the Zoroastrian Arbiter's Bridge, a narrow 'bridge of dread', Hading's bridge, and the guarded bridge over Giǫll.

label: Gates and gatekeeper of the underworld
description: The house of the dead has strong gates, kept by a doorkeeper who checks names and prevents return: gates of Hel, Yama and Hades, Aiakos, Ossetic Aminon, Baltic doors.

label: Dog guarding the realm of the dead
description: A dog (or two) of the underworld lord guards the entrance: Cerberus, Yama's two four-eyed spotted dogs (śabála- possibly from *śarbára- = Κέρβερος), Avestan bridge dogs, Norse Garm, Baltic and Albanian echoes.

label: Otherworld pastures and herds
description: Pastoral Indo-Europeans imagined pastures and herds in the afterlife: Hittite pasture prayer and 'go to the meadow', Vedic cattle-pasture of Yama, Yima 'having good herds', Homeric meadow, Latvian spirits' cows.

label: Going to join the fathers
description: Dying means joining the majority, and specifically one's own dead fathers; Yama gatherer of peoples; Thieme's etymology of Hades as 'he who presides over meeting up'.

label: Annual return and dismissal of the dead
description: At seasonal festivals ancestral souls return, are fed, then formally sent away: Vedic Fathers' cake ritual, Fravashis, Athenian Chytroi, Roman Parentalia and Lemuria, Samain, Yule, Slavic dzjady, Baltic All Souls.

label: Fame as transcendence of death
description: Mortals outlive death only through fame: the name and repute survive while cattle, kin and riches perish; this, more than afterlife rewards, motivated warriors and rulers.

label: Fame as possession placed on a person
description: Fame is a property of the famed person, conferred by a god or self-imposed, idiomatically with the verb 'place' in Graeco-Aryan.

label: Fames of men as subject of song
description: The bards' subject is the 'fames of men', famous exploits, paralleled by Vedic plural śrávāṃsi for Indra's deeds and Old Irish 'fames of chariot-warriors'.

label: Name and fame; naming
description: Fame is bound to one's name: 'famous name' collocations, a 'name-fame' compound, an inherited phrase for name-giving with 'place', and an inherited 'dear name' for a distinguishing surname.

label: Two-part heroic compound names
description: Compound personal names, built like poetic epithets from warrior-society vocabulary, show conservative correspondences across traditions (hero-minded, Zeus-born, -king, conquer, battle-wolf, horse names).

label: Fame-names (*ƙlewes-, *ƙluto-)
description: Names containing 'fame' or 'famous' abound and often match poetic phrases: good, wide, true, god-given, far fame; famed father, famed king; some 250 Greek -kles names.

label: Fame won in combat
description: Battle is the prime arena for winning fame: Maruts as fame-seekers, Zoroastrian 'good fame', Hector and Achilles, Tyrtaeus, Igor, Gododdin, Táin, Beowulf, Norse and Saxo verses.

label: Choosing fame over long life
description: A typical epic motif: the hero is offered a long inglorious life or a short glorious one and chooses glory (Achilles, Karna, the Narts, Cú Chulainn, Cethern, Cynddylig).

label: Poetry confers and sustains fame
description: Lasting fame depends on poems; the poet's fame and the patron's are intertwined (Ibycus, Pindar, Gododdin, Irish bardic verse); Kleio as Muse.

label: Patronymic as verse-filling formula
description: Poetry uses patronymics as epithets and kennings; a shared verse pattern puts the name with a speech verb, then 'son/daughter of X' (Greek, Old High German, Old English, Norse, Russian).

label: Thesaurus of fame: a formulaic system
description: Inherited fame phrases form a semantically complementary system of predicates: good or bad, great, wide, high, unfailing/undying/unageing; extending to heaven and, perhaps, to the end of the world.

label: Fame reaching heaven / lasting to world's end
description: Fame's height reaches the sky (Vedic, Homeric) and its duration may last as long as earth, sun, mountains or the world (Greek, Indian, Welsh, Irish, Norse), though the latter trope is thinly attested.

label: Poet as praise-maker
description: The poet's core role as conferrer of praise on gods and men; Celtic 'bard' analysed as an old compound 'praise-maker' matching an Indo-Iranian phrase for offering praises.

label: Poet as seer and inspired one
description: Poets as prophets or seers with special knowledge, possibly via altered consciousness or frenzy; terms for seer, sage and possessed/inspired poet across Celtic, Italic, Germanic and Graeco-Aryan.

label: Eulogist and herald terms
description: Agent nouns for the praise-singer shared by Indo-Iranian and Greek: Vedic stotṛ́ / Avestan staotar matching Greek στεῦται, and Vedic kārú- matching Greek κήρυξ.

label: High status and hereditary training of poets
description: Poetry was a specialist, often hereditary profession needing long training; master poets enjoyed near-royal status and addressed patrons almost as equals.

label: Poet as spouse of the patron
description: The poet-patron bond imagined as quasi-conjugal: the Indian purohita- installed in a marriage-like rite, Irish and Welsh poets figured as the patron's spouse or lover.

key_terms.term: spouse or lover of his patron
The poet as spouse of his patron

label: Rewards of horses and cattle for poems
description: Patrons repay praise with gifts of horses, cattle, chariots and women, and receive further praise for liberality; stinginess is publicized. Shared by Vedic, Celtic and echoed in Greek.

label: Ancient vocabulary for song and singing
description: Roots for song and singing with wide distribution: Hittite-Vedic-Greek song word, *geh₁, *sengʷʰ, *kan, the laud/Lied set, and Graeco-Aryan ἀείδω~vad-, erg~arká-.

label: Poetry as formal utterance and recital
description: Roots for speaking applied to poetic utterance: *wekʷ (ἔπος, vácas-, ukthám, vacatašti-, Irish anocht ~ Vedic anukta-) and *sekʷ for public recital and narrative.

label: Poetry as recall (memory and the Muse)
description: Composition and recitation conceived as calling to mind, via the root *men; the Muse and Moneta as the one who reminds; Germanic and Slavonic poets 'recall' old lore.

label: Not being unmindful
description: Inverted recall motif: the poet declares he will not forget or leave unremembered his subject, in Homeric Hymns and early Irish and British praise-poems.

key_terms.term: It is not fitting to forget

label: Poetry as making
description: Poetic composition expressed with the plainest verbs for 'make' (Greek τεύχειν, ποιεῖν; Latin facere; Vedic kṛ), with links to Irish duan and creth.

label: Poetry as profitable craft
description: Poetry viewed as a professional craft yielding gain: Welsh cerdd and Irish cerd 'craft; poetry; poet' are cognate with Greek κέρδος 'profit'.

label: Poetry as weaving
description: Composing a song described as weaving or plaiting, with threads and looms, in Indo-Iranian, Greek, Celtic and Germanic poetry.

label: Poetry as carpentry
description: The poet as carpenter or joiner of song via the root *teƙs (Vedic takṣ, Avestan taš, Greek τέκτων), Welsh 'carpenters of song', Norse smiðr and timber imagery.

label: Ship of song
description: The completed song as a vessel that ferries gods or the poet's thought across water; Vedic, Pindaric/Bacchylidean nautical imagery and Norse kennings for poetry as a ship.

label: Chariot of song
description: The hymn as a well-made chariot built, yoked and driven, and poetic contest as chariot race; Vedic, Gathic and Greek (Muses' car), with Chariot Nome and 'pedestrian' prose.

label: Song travels a path through gates
description: Graeco-Aryan idea that the song moves forward on a course: set on the path of song, gates of song opened, roads made smooth for the new hymn.

label: Let the song go forth
description: Third-person imperative wish that the song or praise 'go forth', shared by Vedic etu and Greek ἴτω.

label: Flying, winged song
description: Song or words conceived as flying through the air like birds; winged words and songs that make the honorand fly.

label: Song as arrow
description: The song shot like an arrow from a bow at its target, in Vedic, Atharvan, Mahabharata passages and Pindar's arrows of praise.

label: Inherited syllabic quantitative metre
description: Graeco-Aryan (and MIE) verse of fixed syllable count, caesura, regulated cadence, acatalectic/catalectic pairs and four/five-syllable protasis; Vedic octosyllable ~ glyconic; reflexes in Saturnian, Irish, Slavonic.

label: Alliteration as occasional ornament
description: Alliteration as an intermittent, non-constitutive feature of Indo-European verse, becoming structural where initial stress arose (Italic, Irish, Germanic).

label: Metrical terminology: measure, foot, turn
description: Shared technical vocabulary: measuring the song (Vedic mā, Greek μέτρα), verse as foot or step (pada/pāda, πούς, βάσις), and verse as turn (vṛttam, uersus, στροφή).

label: Poetic prose
description: Elevated non-metrical style with parallelism and contrived order for prayers, ritual, rhetoric and narrative: Vedic mantras, Avestan Yasna Haptanghaiti, Latin/Umbrian litanies, Hittite ritual, Irish rosc.

label: Verse in a prose setting
description: Narratives in prose framing older fixed verse speeches or songs (Brahmanas, Jatakas, sagas, Eddic prose links, Homeric Epigrams).

label: Hymns and praise of patrons
description: Poet's twin duty to celebrate gods and men; invocatory hymns with mythic narrative, and eulogy of the sacrificing patron, his ancestry and comparison with past heroes.

key_terms.term: the doings of men and gods

label: Lament and consolation by examples
description: Poets lament dead patrons; consolation by reciting a series of past misfortunes that were endured or passed, in Greek, Old English and Norse.

label: Heroic narrative of men's renown
description: Lays on past warriors' deeds, sung before battle and at feasts; the 'renowns of men' as subject, probably an MIE institution, with possible inherited ample epic style.

label: Dialogue songs and personation
description: Poems consisting of characters' speeches or dialogues in alternating stanzas without narrator markers, including erotic man-woman dialogues; old in Vedic and widespread.

label: Poet's power of invective
description: The poet who can praise can also blame and curse; satire with magical force (Irish, Norse níðvísur, Greek iambographers, Roman malum carmen).

label: Verse as codification of knowledge
description: Verse used to fix and transmit catalogues, genealogies, laws and gnomic precepts; catalogue poetry and Norse þulur.

label: Assemblies with poets
description: Periodic popular assemblies at which poets performed and entertained; Celtic assemblies held with music, ancestors of eisteddfodau, Irish Tailtiu.

label: Poetic contests
description: Competition among poets for prizes or in question-and-answer and riddle duels of wisdom, in Vedic, Greek, Irish and Norse.

label: Completing a half-verse
description: Agonistic test linking India, Greece and Ireland: one poet sets a paradoxical half-verse and the rival must complete it sensibly.

label: Head forfeited in wisdom contest
description: The loser of a contest of wisdom forfeits his life: head bursts in Upanishad, defeated seer dies, giant wagers his head in Vafþrúðnismál.

label: Gods as 'the celestials'
description: The general IE word for god derives from the root for the bright sky, so the gods are by name the heavenly ones; the heavenly location persists even where the word was replaced.

label: Other words for 'god'
description: Regional words for god are explained as 'those worshipped with libations' (Germanic), 'dispenser' (Iranian, Slavonic), and a root of sacral sense (Greek theos, Italic temple/holiday words).

label: Invoking 'all the gods'
description: Rather than a fixed canon, gods are invoked collectively as 'all the gods', or one chief god is named with 'the other gods' appended; at least Graeco-Aryan.

label: Upper and lower gods
description: Heaven is the seat of the gods, yet divisions into gods of heaven and of earth (Hittite, Greek, Italic, Gaulish) or three tiers (Vedic) occur, probably informally rather than as doctrine.

label: Gods heavenly, men earthly
description: Humans are named 'the earthly ones' from the word for earth, in polar contrast to the celestial gods; the pairing 'gods and men' is kept with the original roots in several branches.

label: The two races: gods and men
description: Gods and men are spoken of as two 'races' or 'kinds', with cognate words for 'race' (jánas-, genos, kin) used in Vedic, Greek and Germanic.

label: Immortal and unageing gods
description: Gods are essentially deathless and ageless; 'immortal gods', 'all the immortals', 'immortals and mortals' and 'immortal and unageing' recur in Vedic, Avestan and Greek.

label: Tireless and sleepless gods
description: Cosmic deities are called untiring, and watchful gods never sleep; a cognate 'unsleeping' epithet joins Vedic, Avestan and Greek.

label: Many names and secret names
description: Gods are 'many-named', yet have one true, sometimes secret name that knowing confers power; the Veda and Greek poetry speak of hidden divine names.

label: Celebrated and superlative epithets
description: Gods are styled 'renowned' with derivatives of the 'hear/fame' root, and divine epithets favour superlatives such as 'highest', 'greatest', 'best'.

label: Being dear to the gods
description: Gods are amoral powers whom one must have as friends; prayers and personal names express being 'dear to' or 'friend of' a god.

label: Gods as kings, fathers, herdsmen
description: Divine relations to people are framed in human social terms: gods are kings, fathers, and shepherds or cowherds of men.

label: Givers of good things
description: Gods are givers; a specific predicate 'giver(s) of good things' is shared by Vedic, Avestan and Greek epic, with echoes in Slavonic and Baltic divine names.

label: Gods walking among men in disguise
description: Gods roam the earth in human form testing men; they betray themselves by eyes or gait, by physical weight, may declare 'I am X', and men may be granted sight to recognize them.

label: Deification by animate gender
description: Things become deities by being cast in the animate (later masculine or feminine) gender: neuter 'contract' becomes Mitra, 'loveliness' becomes Venus, animate fire and water become gods.

label: Agent-noun divine names
description: Functional gods named by agent nouns from verbal roots (Savitr, Tvashtr, Alastor, Jupiter's titles, Roman agricultural godlets): the naming method, not any individual name, is old.

label: 'Lord of' names in *-nos/*-nā
description: A suffix *-nos, feminine *-nā, forms divine and human titles meaning 'lord/mistress of' (Ouranos, Neptunus, Woden, Epona, Perkunas); the type is inherited.

label: Master/mistress titles with *potis
description: In the eastern area 'lord/lady of' is expressed with *potis/*potnih2 compounds and phrases, both human (master of house, clan) and divine (Brhaspati, potnia, Lithuanian -patis gods).

label: Minor role of goddesses
description: Goddesses were marginal in IE theology; natural entities and consorts named from husbands by suffix are inherited types, while goddess prominence in Europe may reflect substrate.

label: Scarcity of divine Mothers
description: Mother-titled goddesses are rare in the Graeco-Aryan area but abundant in western and northern Europe, likely substrate influence; perhaps only Mother Earth was IE.

label: *Aryomen
description: A god embodying 'Aryan-ness' and social, marital ties, reflected in Vedic Aryaman, Avestan Airyaman and Irish Eremon, possibly Germanic *ermana-.

label: Mistress of good things (Vesuna)
description: The 'good things' given by gods yield Vedic vasupati- and the Vasus, and an Italo-Celtic goddess Vesuna, 'mistress of good things'.

label: Frigg and 'beloved'
description: Germanic Frigg derives from an adjective 'dear, beloved' that in the Veda is an epithet of Dawn; whether an IE goddess *Priya existed is doubtful.

label: Hearth goddess and Liber/Eleuthera
description: Greek Hestia matches Roman Vesta, and Roman Liber/Libera match a reconstructed Greek Eleuthera; these reflect Graeco-Italic tradition from central Europe.

label: Divinities of horses
description: Mycenaean 'Mistress of horses', Celtic Epona, Vedic asvapati-, the horse-associated Divine Twins and Illyrian Menzanas suggest IE divinities linked to horses.

label: Veles equation rejected
description: The proposed linking of Slavonic Veles, Lithuanian Velinas, Varuna, Ullr and others via a root 'see' is rejected by West as unfounded.

label: Heteronymous functional homologues
description: Gods with unrelated names but overlapping functions: war-gods who protect fields, archer-healer gods (Apollo, Rudra), and Apollo-Odin-Lug parallels that West attributes to shamanistic diffusion.

label: The mighty infant god
description: A god matures at once: newborn Indra, Zeus, Apollo, Hermes and Norse infant gods act as warriors or perform feats within days of birth.

label: The god's characteristic weapon
description: Gods are imagined holding a typical weapon, expressed in compound epithets like 'vajra-handed', 'arrow-handed' (Vedic and Greek), and magic rods or clubs that kill or revive.

label: The gods' assembly
description: Gods meet and debate in council on high mountains or in their enclosure, sitting on individual seats and rising for the chief god.

label: Divine locomotion
description: Gods travel in giant strides, with wind-shoes or magic sandals, by horse and chariot, or by flying in bird form.

label: Golden gods and their gear
description: Gods, their hair, horses, chariots, weapons, armour, houses and thrones are of gold, with matching 'gold-' compounds in Vedic, Avestan and Greek.

label: The divine smith
description: Craftsman gods (Hephaestus, Tvashtr and the Rbhus, Kurdalagon, Goibniu, Baltic sky-smith) make the chief god's weapon and are tied to the gods' drink; a common prototype is possible but weak.

label: Food of immortality
description: Gods do not eat human food; their special food of 'non-dying' (amrtam, ambrosia) and nectar ('overcoming death') keeps them immortal, also feeding their horses.

label: Bird fetches or steals the elixir
description: The divine elixir lies in a guarded, hard-to-reach place; a bird brings it to the chief god losing a feather or member, or a god in bird form steals it back.

label: The language of the gods
description: Certain things have one name among gods and another among men (or other orders of beings), a poetic conceit for marking rare or elevated vocabulary.

label: Former gods and divine wars
description: An earlier set of 'former gods' was displaced and confined below; wars between orders of gods (Titans, Asuras, Vanir, Fomoire) are suggestive of an IE motif.

label: Assaults on heaven
description: Beings who try to climb to heaven, often by piling up mountains or objects, are struck down, affirming the unbridgeable gap between celestials and terrestrials.

label: Dedicated storm-god distinct from sky-god
description: The IE thunderer was originally a separate deity from the bright-sky god *Dyeus; Zeus and Jupiter absorbed the storm role, while most branches keep a distinct storm-god.

label: Perkunas name family ('master of the oak')
description: The Baltic thunder-god's name is analysed as oak-word *perkʷu- plus the divine 'master of' suffix -no-, with cognate names spread across Germanic, Slavic and possibly Indic, though no single prototype is securely reconstructable.

label: Thunder-god and the oak
description: The storm-god characteristically strikes oaks, stores fire in them, and owns sacred oaks or groves: Baltic, Slavic, Greek (Dodona), Roman and Norse evidence.

label: Wooded mountains as the thunder-god's realm
description: Derivatives of the Perkunas name denote forested mountains (Hercynian forest, Gothic fairguni, Slavic 'wooded hill'); Norse Fiǫrgynn/Fiǫrgyn, Thor's mother, may personify that landscape.

label: 'Striker' etymology, taboo variants and Keraunos
description: Perun as 'the Striker' from *per; taboo deformation of the thunderer's name; Greek Keraunos possibly the faded name of an independent Greek thunder-god surviving as Zeus' thunderbolt and epithet.

label: Thunder-god's goat-drawn car
description: Perkunas and Thor ride behind goats (the snipe's goat-like bleat presages storms); Zeus' epithet aigiochos originally meant 'riding a goat', with αἴξ cognate to Lithuanian ožys.

label: Red beard and beard-shaking
description: A reddish or fiery beard marks the IE thunder-god (Perkunas, Perun, Indra, Thor, Vahagn); Indra and Thor shake their beards, with cognate verbs.

label: Storm-god as bellowing bull and rain-fertilizer
description: Parjanya (and Indra, Perkunas) appear as bellowing bulls; Parjanya fertilizes Earth with rain-seed, taking the sky-father's role; the bull's bellow parallels thunder.

label: Thunder-god as prodigious eater and drinker
description: Indra, Heracles and Thor share gargantuan appetites for meat and drink, part of a brawny, violent champion profile.

label: Storm-god born through his mother's side
description: Indra refuses normal birth and exits sideways from his mother's ribs; the Hittite Storm-god emerges from Kumarbi by 'the good place'; possibly lightning bursting from the cloud's side.

label: Threefold thunder: sound, flash, bolt
description: The storm's effects are split into three agents (thunder, lightning, bolt): Hesiod's Cyclopes who arm Zeus, and Pērkons' nine sons in triads; Thor as 'Thunder' son of Fiǫrgynn fits this pattern.

label: Strength and victory accompany the god
description: Personified Power/Strength follows the god wherever he goes: Thor (Snorri), Indra with the goddess Táviṣī, Zeus with Kratos and Bia; West hesitates to posit a common archetype.

label: Recital catalogues of the god's deeds
description: Hymns and poems list the champion god's famous exploits: Rigvedic Indra hymns, Greek Heracles epics and odes, skaldic praises of Thor.

label: The thunder-weapon (club, mace, hammer)
description: The storm-god wields a crushing club/hammer of stone or metal, often smith-made, bright, sharp, many-edged: vajra, Avestan vazra, keraunos, Miǫllnir; it breaks the enemy's head and scorches him.

label: Returning weapon and thunderstones
description: The bolt is renewable either because the weapon returns to the god's hand (Miǫllnir, Perkunas' hammer, the Dagda) or because fallen thunderstones (prehistoric celts) supply inexhaustible missiles with protective magic.

label: Lightning makes fire between two stones
description: Belorussian Piarun flashes lightning from between two stones, as Indra 'generated fire between two stones'.

key_terms.term: he who generated fire between two stones

label: Thunder-god slays the water dragon
description: A monstrous serpent lies in or blocks the waters; the thunder-god smashes its head with his weapon, releasing streams, and it sinks into the waters/darkness: Vṛtra, Typhoeus, the Miðgarð Serpent.

label: Vṛtra-smasher title (vṛtrahán- / Vərəθraγna-)
description: Indra's frequent title 'obstacle-smasher' matches the Avestan victory-god Vərəθraγna; originally a battle epithet from which the monster Vṛtra was abstracted; the Armenian Vahagn continues it as dragon-slayer.

label: Serpent encircling the flood/world
description: Vṛtra 'lay round the flood' and the Miðgarð Serpent 'lies round all lands'; the dragon-killing may be past yet unresolved, the monster still lying hidden in the waters.

label: Water-blocking/drought demon and spring-guarding serpents
description: Variants of the water-serpent: Avestan drought demon Apaoša 'water-blocker', Python at a Delphic spring, the many-headed Hydra of springs, Albanian Kulshedra drying streams, Perun's dragon forming the Dnieper.

label: Three-headed monster killed, cattle freed
description: A three-headed (six-eyed) monster holding cows is slain and his herd driven off: Viśvarūpa by Trita Āptya/Indra, Aži Dahāka by Θraētaona, Geryon (with dog Orthos) by Heracles, Cacus by Hercules/Garanus.

label: 'Third' as a hieratic hero-name
description: The dragon-slayer Trita/Θrita 'Third' (Āptya, 'of the Waters') may be paralleled by Greek 'Third Saviour', Tritogeneia, Norse þriði; a coded hieratic name.

label: Cattle hidden beyond the world-river
description: Stolen cows are kept beyond the world-encircling stream (Paṇis beyond the Rasā, tracked by the dog Saramā; Geryon beyond Ocean); related to cows released from a rock as the dawn.

label: Colossus unmoved by seduction, felled by the storm-god
description: A huge (stone) adversary grows to threaten the gods, resists erotic enticement, and is finally struck down: Triśiras, Hittite/Hurrian Ullikummi, Norse Hrungnir with his stone head.

label: Wind gods
description: Winds, named from the root 'blow' with animate masculine nouns, are personified and receive cult in Hittite, Vedic (Vāyu, Vāta), Iranian, Greek, Slavic and Baltic tradition, often linked to horses and chariots.

label: Fire as a deity
description: The animate fire-word suits fire as an active divine principle: Vedic Agni, Avestan Ātar, Lithuanian holy fire Ugnis/Gabija, Latvian Mother of Fire, Norse Logi, Germanic 'Volcanus'.

label: Fire god as son of the sky-god
description: Agni is son of Dyaus, Ātar son of Ahura Mazdā (perhaps adapted), Hephaestus son of Zeus.

label: Hearth goddess and perpetual fire
description: The sacral/domestic hearth is under a female 'Burning' deity (Scythian Tabiti, Hestia, Vesta), with perpetual fires, round altars, and rekindling by wood-drilling as for Agni.

label: Fire gods Volcanus and Hephaestus
description: Marginal male fire-gods: Greek Hephaestus (also 'fire' as common noun) and Roman Volcanus, 'master of' a fire-word, matched by Ossetic Wärgon; both later cast as smiths.

label: Hearth cult and 'master of the house'
description: The hearth as the home's centre receives offerings; brides circle it three times; the hearth-fire god bears the title 'master of the house' in Vedic, Avestan, Lithuanian and perhaps Mycenaean.

label: Fire as devourer
description: Fire is pictured as eating, with teeth and jaws, omnivorous, in Vedic, Greek and Germanic poetry (also Near Eastern); Logi wins an eating contest.

label: The Fire in the Waters (Grandson of the Waters)
description: A fiery divine being dwells in and is nurtured by the female Waters (Apām napāt, Agni found in the rivers), with possible Greek, Armenian (Vahagn from the burning reed) and Norse kenning reflexes.

label: Shining sovereign glory held in the waters
description: Apąm napāt guards the radiant sovereign glory in lake Vourukaša, which Fraŋrasyan dives for in vain; compare Theseus diving for Minos' gold ring among fire-bright Nereids.

label: Fire hidden in trees by the lightning-god
description: Fire latent in wood, especially fire-stick trees, is believed lodged there by lightning; Agni hides in waters and plants and is found (śamī tree); Zeus withholds fire from the ash-trees.

label: Theft/bringing of fire and the first sacrifice
description: Fire is snatched from heaven and brought to men in connection with the first sacrifice and ancestor of mankind: Mātariśvan for Manu; Prometheus 'Seizer' (pra-math-), father of Deucalion; Phoroneus. A Graeco-Aryan myth.

label: The holy Waters
description: Terrestrial waters are venerated collectively ('the Waters', 'Rivers and Springs') in Hittite, Indo-Iranian, Greek and other traditions; the animate water-word became feminine.

label: Rivers as gods, mothers, bulls and fathers
description: Individual rivers are personified and worshipped: bull-horned Greek river-gods who father heroes, Father Tiber, Rhine as ancestor, Russian 'Mother Dniepr', Baltic Upinis and Latvian river-Mothers; prayers to rivers when crossing.

label: Neptunus, Nechtan and the harmful sacred well
description: Neptune as original god of fresh waters ('master of wetness'); Dumézil's link to Apām napāt and Irish Nechtan, whose eye-destroying well floods (compare Baltic Golbe), is judged ingenious but doubtful.

label: Thunder-god in curses
description: Popular imprecations invoke the thunder-god to strike or kill the cursed person, in Lithuanian (Perkunas) and Russian, Ukrainian, Slovenian (Perun).

key_terms.term: ‘may Perun (or Perun’s bolt) kill you (or take you)’

label: Invocatory hymn as public ceremonial genre
description: The poet's hymn addresses a deity on behalf of a patron or community at a public ceremony, usually with an offering, petitioning blessings; evidence mainly Indo-Iranian and Greek, hence secure at Graeco-Aryan level with hints deeper.

label: Opening: god's name plus first-person performative 'I invoke'
description: Hymns begin by identifying the addressee: the god's name in the accusative (or 'thee' plus vocative) governed by a first-person verb 'I/we invoke, venerate, sing', found in Vedic, Avestan, Greek, Latin, Umbrian and Gaulish.

label: The god invoked first (and not forgotten)
description: The invoked deity is declared to be called first, before others, or first and last in the singer's thoughts; the singer vows never to forget the god, in Vedic and Greek hymns.

key_terms.term: πρῶτον μὲν εὐχῆι τῆιδε πρεσβεύω θεῶν

label: Paired deities: vocative plus nominative with *kʷe
description: When two gods are invoked together, Vedic and Greek address one in the vocative and append the other in the nominative with the copula from *kʷe, as if one were second and the other third person.

label: Opening question: which god shall we praise, and how?
description: A hymn may open by asking which deity to honour or how to praise him, then answer it, in Rigveda, Pindar and the Homeric Hymn to Apollo.

key_terms.term: τίνα θεόν, τίν̓ ἥρωα, τίνα δ̓ ἄνδρα κελαδήσομεν

label: Epithets and anaphoric relative clauses of praise
description: The god's name is followed by honorific epithets and a chain of relative clauses ('whom...', 'who...'), in Vedic, Avestan, Old Persian royal inscriptions, Hittite prayers and later Greek hymns.

description: Hymns predicate that whoever the deity favours succeeds, and whoever honours or sacrifices to him is rewarded, in Vedic, Avestan and Hesiodic passages.

label: Mythical narrative within the hymn
description: Unlike Near Eastern hymnody, Vedic and Greek hymns motivate praise by allusion to the god's past deeds and birth, introduced by 'I will tell forth'; the allusive, vignette style is probably Graeco-Aryan if not Indo-European.
