devā́nāṃ nú vayáṃ jā́nā | prá vocāma vipanyáyā

label: Gods rejoice and the world trembles at a god's birth
description: At a new deity's birth the other gods rejoice or marvel and heaven and earth tremble (Indra, Athena); the Greek and Vedic verbs for 'tremble' may be cognate.

label: Aufreihlied: serial listing of a god's or hero's exploits
description: Hymns list the deity's accomplishments in series (Indra, the Aśvins, Kərəsāspa, Heracles' Labours, Thor's giant-killings); the shared technique for storm-god hymns may reflect an Indo-European tradition.

key_terms.term: this Indra did exalted by the Soma

label: 'Hear us': the call to the god to hear
description: Prayers ask the god to hear, using reflexes of *ƙlu in Indo-Iranian, Greek and Messapic, often with vocative and 'me/my prayer'; also third-person 'let X hear', 'hear well', and Latin audi Iuppiter.

label: Hearing means granting
description: 'Hear' implies 'hear and respond': in Homer a prayer is followed by 'and the god heard him', meaning fulfilment; a Russian bylina river likewise 'gave ear'.

label: 'Look on us': appeal for the god's gaze
description: The god is asked to direct his eyes on the suppliants, in Hittite, Vedic, Avestan, Greek, Old Norse and an early Slavic sacrificial cry.

key_terms.term: Deus ad nos et animas [animal?] cornutum respice

label: 'Come': summoning the god to the rite
description: The deity is implored to come to the ceremony or to help, often coupled with 'hear', in Luwian, Vedic, Avestan, Greek and Latvian.

label: Appeal to past responses ('if ever before...')
description: The appeal is strengthened by recalling that the god has answered similar calls before ('as before, so now too'), in Vedic, Homeric, Sappho, and an old Russian harvest prayer.

label: 'Come with': the god arrives with companions
description: The god is asked to come together with other deities (instrumental/comitative in Vedic and Avestan, σύν + dative in Greek); rivers are bidden come with their waves, exactly as in a Roman prayer to the Tiber.

label: Gods hear from afar; listing possible whereabouts
description: Gods hear and come from any distance; the singer covers alternatives ('far or near', a series of places, 'from heaven, from earth'), a pattern in Hittite, Vedic, Avestan and Greek.

key_terms.term: ā́ yātu Índro divá ā́ pṛthivyā́
a god hears even from afar
whether you are far or near

label: Tripartite structure: invocation, praise, petition
description: After invocation and praise come requests for boons, an arguably Indo-European structure exemplified by the Hittite Telibinu hymn; petitions are usually communal and general, often closing the hymn.

label: Herds and men as objects of protection
description: The ancient polar formula 'men and cattle' figures in prayers as the collective to be protected, in Umbrian, Latin and Indo-Iranian (after Watkins).

label: Arguments urging the petition: 'this lies in your power'
description: The suppliant urges that the request lies within the god's power (Vedic, Homeric, Latvian); he may also recall past offerings (Iliad, Hittite, Indian epic), a motif West thinks possibly Semitic-influenced.

label: Etymological play on the god's name
description: The god's name or title is punningly invoked to imply his power to do what is asked (Savitṛ 'stimulate', Apollo 'destroy', Lykeios 'be wolfish'), in Vedic and Greek.

label: Hope that the god is gratified by the hymn
description: Especially at the hymn's end the singer prays that the deity may take pleasure in the praise or offering, in Vedic and Greek.

label: Poet's self-reference at the hymn's end
description: The closing of a hymn is where the poet names himself, his family or patron (Vedic Rishis, the blind Chian of the Hymn to Apollo, Bacchylides, Timotheus), part of an old Graeco-Aryan hymn tradition.

label: Divine will versus magical compulsion
description: Prayer concedes 'as the gods wish, so it will be' (near-identical Vedic and Avestan phrasing); spells instead compel, working automatically if correctly worded, hence fixed esoteric texts. Indo-Europeans evidently practised such magic.

key_terms.term: Spells and incantations, on the other hand, were esoteric knowledge

label: Incantation as song
description: Spells are named with song vocabulary: Greek 'singing over', Italic and Celtic root *kan- (Latin carmen, Irish canaid), Norse lióð and galdr; Odin catalogues his eighteen spells.

label: Stylistic marks of incantations
description: Spells use metre, repetition, anaphora with increasing phrase length, alliteration, rhyme, tricola, paired alliterative phrases, polar expressions and syzygies of near-synonyms to leave no loophole.

key_terms.term: hvé ec fyrbýð, hvé ec fyrirbanna

label: Nine and thrice nine as sacral numbers
description: Ritual repetition is formalized numerically; nine and thrice nine recur widely in Greek, Roman, Germanic, Baltic and Irish religious and magical contexts, suggesting a traditional sacral quantity.

label: Herbs and spells combined
description: Magical operations pair incantation with potent herbs gathered under special rules; Indian epic speaks of the power of spells and herbs.

label: Spell recounting the herb's discovery
description: In India and Italy the charm addresses the herb with its history (found, dug, culled, eaten) to warrant its fitness and bind it to its task; West finds the parallelism astonishing.

key_terms.term: suparṇás tvā́nv avindata, sūkarás tvākhanan nasā́

label: Binding spells
description: Harmful magic binds its victim with a performative 'I bind', with counterspells to release bonds: Varuna's fetters in the Atharvaveda, the Erinyes' binding hymn, Odin's fetter-spell, the first Merseburg charm.

label: Stabbing by malediction; root *(s)tig
description: Curses picture piercing the victim, rooted in stabbing images; the root *(s)tig 'pierce' may have had this association (Greek papyri, Neo-Phrygian tomb curses, Gaulish 'bewitch').

label: Enumerating body parts in curses and cures
description: To make the spell comprehensive, the victim's or patient's body parts are listed one by one, in Atharvavedic curses and healing, Greek and Latin defixiones, and Christianized Irish prayers.

key_terms.term: From your eyes, from your nose, from your ears, from your chin

label: Three kinds of healing: knife, herb, spell
description: The Avesta distinguishes knife-, herb- and spell-healers; Pindar credits Asclepius with incantation, drugs and surgery; Darmesteter inferred an Indo-European medical triad, though methods were combined.

label: Disease counted in multiples (seventy-seven, ninety-nine)
description: An Atharvavedic charm counts sores in fives-and-fifties to nines-and-nineties, coinciding remarkably with German charms against seventy-seven or 'ninety-nine and seventy-seven' diseases.

label: Driving disease out part by part; the disease-worm
description: Disease is expelled step by step from inner to outer parts (marrow, bone, flesh, skin) until it leaves the body; illness is blamed on worms, slain by performative 'I slay the worm' in Vedic, Germanic and Irish.

key_terms.term: Go out, worm, with your nine wormlings!
limb by limb, joint by joint

label: Legendenzauber: mythic narrative validating a spell
description: Healing charms open with a mythical precedent that establishes their efficacy (Atharvavedic charms, German folk spells, both Merseburg charms with Wodan and goddesses).

key_terms.term: Phol and Wodan were riding to the woods
Ibant aliquando tres puellae in via virente

label: 'Bone to bone, blood to blood' healing formula
description: Healing charms join like to like ('bone to bone, blood to blood, joint to joint'): second Merseburg charm, later European versions, Old Irish Míach, Atharvaveda (Kuhn), even a Hittite-Luwian ritual; a traditional Indo-European figure of polyptoton.

ault fri halt di ocus féith fri féth

label: 'Stand upright': the formula of successful healing
description: The cured patient is told 'stand firm upright', words matching Pindar's Asclepius setting patients upright; in both traditions the phrase expresses successful healing.

label: War-band of young warriors
description: Bands of unmarried young men living on society's margins, following a leader on raids; a pan-European institution named by an inherited word for 'war-band/army' and its derivative 'war-band leader'.

label: Warriors as wolves; battle frenzy
description: Frenzied warriors fighting naked or in animal skins are assimilated to wolves; 'wolf' names and metaphors for warriors and outlaws, Homeric lyssa, lycanthropy, and possibly an initiatory wolf-band institution.

label: Cattle raid
description: Driving off others' herds is an easy route to wealth and a celebrated form of aggression in Vedic, Iranian, Greek, Irish and British tradition.

label: Sacking the stronghold
description: Breaching an enemy hill-fort brings signal glory; cognate words for 'fort' and epithets for the rampart-breaker or city-sacker (Indra, Greek heroes), and the 'hundred strongholds' as a mark of great warfare.

label: Siege as 'sitting around'
description: Several branches express besieging with compounds of the verb 'sit' plus 'around/at', all from one root.

label: Chosen warriors
description: A whole corps is praised as individually excellent by calling its members 'chosen' warriors, in Vedic, Welsh, Old English and Latin sources.

label: Hero as man-slayer
description: The hero is fundamentally a killer, bearing 'man-slaying' epithets in Vedic and Greek, and similar labels in Irish.

label: Hero as wall, fortress or pillar
description: The hero shields his people like a protective wall, tower, enclosure or pillar: Greek, Welsh, Irish, Germanic and Armenian metaphors, faded in a Germanic formula meaning 'leader'.

label: Warrior heat and the hero's light
description: Battle fury shows as abnormal body heat, fire or light emanating from the hero's head or body, and grotesque facial distortion.

label: Terrifying war-cry
description: The hero's shout is so loud it routs or kills enemies (Achilles, Bhima, Cu Chulainn, Batradz).

label: Special martial feats
description: Heroes command a formal repertory of expert combat manoeuvres, elaborate in Indian and Irish narrative and faintly hinted in Homer.

label: Delight in battle and fighting in front
description: True heroes rejoice in and thirst for combat (words for 'battle' derived from 'joy') and lead from the front line, in many traditions.

label: Vow of abnegation
description: A hero vows to forgo food, washing, hair-cutting or a seat of honour until vengeance or a goal is achieved.

label: Excellent and famous weapons
description: The warrior's weapons are 'well-made', 'well-shaven', and his fame is linked to them through compound epithets ('spear-famed', 'of the famous bow').

label: Mace, club and uprooted tree
description: An archaic 'smasher' or club marks exceptional heroes; uprooting trees as weapons signals vast strength.

label: Marvellous, named and crafted weapons
description: Unique weapons of superhuman quality: swords so sharp they cut a hair floating on water, weapons with names and histories, forged by special craftsmen or dwarfs.

label: Animate weapons
description: Weapons share their owners' bloodlust, eager to fly or drink blood; some fight by themselves or return to the thrower's hand.

label: Fiery weapons
description: As heat bursts from the hero, his weapons blaze with flame.

label: Oaths by weapons and weapon cult
description: Warriors swear by their weapons; weapons are worshipped as gods (Scythian scimitar, Roman Mars as spear).

key_terms.term: tar mó sciath 7 tar mó cloidim

label: Weapon removed after the hero's death
description: A hero's weapon is so bound to him that it must be cast into sea or lake after him; cf. prehistoric weapon deposits in waters.

label: Horses and men
description: Men and horses are habitually coupled in battle diction across Greek, Iranian, Armenian, Latin, Welsh, Irish and Norse.

label: Poetic epithets of horses
description: An early poetic vocabulary for horses: swift, wind-swift, flying, prize-winning, strong-hooved; the 'master of horses' title.

label: Talking and grieving horses
description: Heroes' horses are wise, prophetic and can converse with them, and grieve at their master's death.

label: Chariot warfare and charioteer
description: Pair-drawn war-chariots (a post-PIE invention) with a charioteer who is the hero's herald, friend and adviser, in Indo-Iranian, Greek and Irish tradition; parallel chariot epithets.

label: Catalogue of forces
description: Battle narratives catalogue contingents and leaders, explicitly declining to name the multitude, or count armies by multiplication.

label: Identification of warriors from a vantage point
description: A Teichoskopia-type scene in which one person describes warriors seen below and another names them (Greek, Indic, Irish, Welsh, Norse).

label: Pre-assigned opponents
description: Before battle, which champion will face which is decided, e.g. at the seven gates of Thebes and Lanka.

label: Arming scene
description: Heroes arm piece by piece, with details of material, decoration and history.

label: Battle from dawn to dusk
description: Fighting begins at dawn and stops at nightfall, often divided at midday; warriors boast 'you will see me tomorrow'; a sleepless hero devises a night raid.

label: Verbal duels before combat
description: Encounters open with taunts: 'who are you?', boasts, 'either I kill you or you me', 'God knows who will win'.

label: Battle exhortations
description: Leaders rouse troops: 'remember your courage', recall boasts made over drink, 'shame, where are you fleeing?', piled imperatives, and cautionary exempla of past heroes.

label: Mass battle imagery
description: Clash of shields, showers of missiles, darkness blinding combatants, polyptoton of rank against rank, one against many, mass kills.

label: Making light for one's side
description: The saviour hero 'makes' or 'becomes' a light for his side, a Graeco-Aryan expression.

label: Gods in battle
description: Gods lead armies, appear in the fray (the Divine Twins on white horses), serve as charioteers, hide heroes in mist or snatch them away; heroes are taken for gods or defy them.

label: Archery motifs
description: Shared Greek-Indic traits: winged and flying arrows, shining bows bent into a circle, rattling quiver, twang, bird-target contest, severed bowstrings.

label: Chariot mishaps
description: Broken shafts, slain charioteers, bolting horses, rescue by another chariot, and empty chariots rattling over the field.

label: Single combat and champion's portion
description: Duels follow a set pattern, may settle a war, take place in a marked-out arena; the victor gets the best cut of meat.

label: Portents and doom of the fated warrior
description: Rains of blood presage death; the doomed man is dazed, deluded by the gods, or bound by a fetter of death.

label: The hero's fall
description: Vomiting blood, embracing the earth, biting the dust, the soul's departure, followers fleeing, earth drinking blood, rivers blocked by corpses, carrion beasts.

label: Vindictive victory
description: Mutilation of the slain enemy: dragging the corpse behind a chariot, head-taking, drinking blood, skull cups.

label: Battle similes
description: Shared simile types: hero as forest fire, sea wave, rock, tree (and felled tree), lion among cattle; enemies flee like deer or clouds.

label: The hero's funeral
description: Lamentation, cremation on a pyre with armour, animals and human victims, gathering bones into an urn, tumulus by the sea, over many days; tumulus burial is older than cremation.

label: Laments for the hero
description: Composed laments by kin, a leader of the wailing with women's responses; widows' fears of captivity and pathetic contrasts.

label: Suttee
description: The widow's voluntary death with her husband, attested in Vedic India, Thrace, Slavs, Balts, Germanic peoples and Armenia.

label: Funeral games and circumequitation
description: Contests, especially horse or chariot races, after a hero's funeral; riding or marching thrice round the pyre or tomb.

label: The 'new song' added to tradition
description: Poets across traditions call their song new or newest, meaning a fresh addition to an inherited body of older praise-poetry rather than a break with it.

label: 'Ancient songs' and archaic diction
description: Several Indo-European cultures honoured traditional poetry as 'ancient songs', and poetic language everywhere favours archaism and formularity over contemporary speech.

label: Hermetic poetic language vs human speech
description: The poet glories in a secret, riddling language understood only by initiates, contrasted with the speech of ordinary humankind (and akin to the 'language of gods').

label: Emphatic word order; patronymic before name
description: Poetic syntax freely moves words into emphatic positions; a widespread inversion puts 'son of Y' before the name X, as in Homeric, Vedic, Avestan, Latin, Irish and Germanic verse.

label: Formula survival through lexical renewal
description: Inherited phrases keep their identity even when constituent words are replaced by newer synonyms, so semantic parallels can be adduced besides strict etymological ones.

label: Inherited poetic compounds
description: Decorative compound epithets are the largest class of poetic words; some cognate formations across languages suggest a shared inherited stock.

label: Prefixed proper names
description: A type of compound attaches an intensifying or pejorative prefix to a proper name ('Great Indra', 'Ill-Paris'); the type, not the examples, may be inherited.

label: Name-substitute kennings: 'son of' and 'slayer of'
description: A hero or god is designated by parentage or kinship ('son of Y'), or by the famous adversary he killed, as with Indra the Vṛtra-slayer.

label: Metaphorical kennings (hand, ship, missiles)
description: Shared periphrases include the hand as 'five-branched', the ship as 'horse of the sea', and battle missiles as an 'iron shower'.

label: Ornamental epithets (epitheta ornantia)
description: Fixed noun-epithet pairs naming a permanent quality recur across traditions: swift messenger, well-clothed woman, shining garments, grey wolf, sweet mead, broad sea, ships.

label: The sun as measure of world and life
description: The sun frames idioms of totality ('as far as the sun sees'), of the inhabited world ('under the sun'), and of being alive ('to see the sun'); birth is coming into the light.

label: Cosmic eternity formulas
description: 'For ever' is expressed as 'as long as sun, moon, heaven or earth endure', in Hittite, Luwian, Indic, Greek and Celtic texts.

label: Birth and begetting idioms
description: Fatherhood is stressed by pairing 'father begetter'; character is expressed as 'your parent bore you to be' or 'the gods made him'; birth as reaching the mother's knees.

label: Menos/manas collocations (spirit, courage)
description: Greek μένος, cognate with Indo-Iranian 'mind', enters inherited collocations: good/bright spirit blown into men, bold spirit, man-spirit, 'vigorous' spirit.

label: Emotion and heart idioms
description: Emotions as external forces; the unyielding have hearts of iron or bronze; inward glee as 'his heart laughed' (Greek, Germanic); other parallels may be areal.

label: Sweet, honeyed and poured speech
description: Poetic utterance is sweet like honey or mead, ambrosial, and is 'poured' out like a libation (root *gˆʰu).

label: Time reckoning: nights and days; 'all days'
description: Durations are counted as 'n nights and n days', especially three; 'all days' means continually or for ever.

label: Battle-cry reaching heaven
description: The noise of battle or a shout is said to reach the sky or clouds, in Greek, Indian epic, Irish and Serbo-Croat poetry.

label: Clothing metaphor (*wes): clad in cloud or valour
description: Gods are clothed in cloud and heroes clad in strength or valour, using the clothing root in Vedic and Homeric diction.

label: Opening call to attention
description: Poems open with 'hear this, people' and an announcement of song, built on the hearing root, in Vedic, Gathic, Eddic and Greek.

label: Story openings: 'There was a king, N his name'
description: Tales begin with initial 'to be' setting place or protagonist, especially 'There was a king, his name N'.

label: Narrator's authority: 'I have heard'; question and answer
description: Lacking Muses, poets cite hearsay ('I have heard', root *ƙlu); or they pose a factual question and answer it themselves.

label: Inherited and Graeco-Aryan similes
description: Few similes are shared: swift as thought, quicker than a blink, multitudes like sand or stars; Greek-Indic like gods, like the moon, bull in the herd; Sappho's moon and sleepless bird.

label: Polar expressions (merisms)
description: Totality is expressed by paired opposites (gods and men, two- and four-footed, herds and men, moving and still); West calls bipolarity the basic structuring principle of IE thought.

label: X and non-X; seen and unseen; male and female
description: Negative compounds yield catch-all pairs (willing/unwilling, seen/unseen), suited to legal and ritual language; prayers cover god or goddess; a middle term may be appended.

label: Past, present and future as totality and uniqueness
description: What was, is and will be expresses universality and the seer's knowledge; 'none was born nor will be' expresses uniqueness, including of matchless crafted weapons.

key_terms.term: τά τ’ ἐόντα τά τ’ ἐσσόμενα πρό τ’ ἐόντα
engi hefir sá orðit ok engi mun verða

label: Positive reinforced by negated opposite
description: A statement is emphasized by adding the negation of its opposite ('true, not false'), notably in Graeco-Aryan, sometimes coining irregular negative nouns.

label: Epanadiplosis (iteration)
description: Immediate repetition of a word, either liturgical-magical to boost potency or mimetic to express repeated or protracted action.

label: Epanalepsis
description: A word or phrase ending one verse is picked up at the start of the next, in Vedic, Homeric, Irish, Norse, Russian and Balkan poetry.

label: Questioner's suggestions negated in turn
description: A questioner proposes possible answers which the respondent rejects one by one before giving the truth, as with Hector asking after Andromache.

key_terms.term: Has she gone to one of her sisters-in-law or mine
she has gone to the great wall of Ilios

label: Anaphora (incl. repeated preverb)
description: Repetition of a key word, often the initially placed verb, two to four times, to stress quantity or a quality; Indo-Iranian and Greek also repeat a preverb with the verb elided.

label: Anaphora of compound first elements
description: Strings of adjectives sharing a prefix, especially good-, ill-, un- and much-, e.g. 'unageing, immortal'.

label: Juxtaposition of opposed terms
description: Opposites, often one negated, are set side by side in different cases (immortals to mortals, impious with pious), or contrasted compounds are opposed.

label: Polyptoton (like terms juxtaposed)
description: Same word in different cases: elatives ('strongest of the strong'), accumulation ('wound upon wound'), reciprocity (god to god, friend to friend), and piled-up battle clashes.

label: The priamel
description: A series of parallel statements foils a final climactic one; Vedic, Rāmāyaṇa and Germanic examples exist, but West finds the evidence too scant to call it Indo-European.

label: Behaghel's Law and the Augmented Triad
description: Shorter elements precede longer; a line of three names with an epithet on the third, notably 'three sons of N' formulas, looks like an inherited catalogue device.
